plan.contextChunk: This figure is a two-part free-body construction, panels (a) and (b), each pairing a small pictorial sketch with an isolated force diagram at its left and a legend of symbol definitions at its right. Both sketches show the same tan incline sloping down to the left, a small salmon block labeled A resting on a larger block labeled B, and a cord running up the slope; a rounded outline circles block A in (a) and block B in (b). In (a), block A is reduced to a black dot on a dashed line standing for the incline surface, carrying four red vectors: N_BA perpendicular to and away from the surface, T up the slope, f_BA down the slope, and w_A vertically down. In (b), block B carries five: N_B perpendicular away from the incline, f_AB and f_B both up the slope, N_AB perpendicular and directed down into the incline, and w_B vertically down. The legends spell the symbols out, among them "N_BA = normal force exerted by B on A" and "f_B = friction force exerted by the incline plane on B". Stacking the two isolations invites comparison of the paired contact forces and the reversed friction directions. The construction demonstrates how to isolate stacked bodies touching two surfaces at once.

interactions.teaches: A free-body diagram is drawn for one selected object only, so arrows from contacts, gravity, and tension appear only if they act directly on that isolated body

interactions.label: Highlight contact-force pair
interactions.teaches: Newton's third-law contact forces come in opposite-direction pairs, but the two forces in a pair belong on different free-body diagrams

interactions.label: Relative sliding tendency
interactions.teaches: Friction along a contact surface is set by the relative sliding tendency at that surface, so reversing the tendency reverses the friction arrows

demo_steps.title: Isolate one block
demo_steps.narration: Click block A or block B in the incline sketch. The selected block and its free-body diagram brighten, emphasizing that the diagram contains only forces acting on that block.

demo_steps.title: Compare the normal pair
demo_steps.narration: With the A-B normal pair highlighted, N_BA appears on block A while N_AB appears on block B. The arrows point in opposite perpendicular directions because each block pushes on the other.

demo_steps.title: Compare the friction pair
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the A-B friction pair. f_BA and f_AB are parallel to the contact surface but point in opposite directions, and they are placed on different isolated bodies.

demo_steps.title: Reverse the sliding tendency
demo_steps.narration: Change the relative sliding tendency and watch the friction arrows reverse along the contact surfaces. This shows that friction opposes relative motion, not simply motion to the left or right.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The same contact produces two opposite forces, but each force must be drawn only on the free-body diagram of the object it acts on.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the figure as two horizontal textbook-style panels stacked vertically. In each panel, place the isolated red-arrow force diagram on the left, the small incline-and-block sketch in the middle, and the symbol-definition legend on the right. Use tan for the incline, tan for block B, salmon for block A, black for labels and cord, gray rounded outlines for the isolated body, and red arrows for forces. Keep the incline angle consistent across both panels. In click isolation mode, brighten the selected panel's isolated body outline and corresponding free-body diagram while fading the other body and unrelated arrows. In contact-pair mode, emphasize N_BA with N_AB for the normal pair or f_BA with f_AB for the friction pair using stronger red or glow, while other force arrows remain visible but muted. In sliding-tendency mode, reverse friction arrows along the A-B contact; also make clear that the incline friction on B depends on B's tendency relative to the plane.

authoredContext:
Two Blocks on an Inclined Plane Construct the free-body diagram for object A and object B in the figure. Assume that the rope pulls object A so that it slides upward, and that object B is sliding down the slope.

Solution We start by creating a diagram for the first object of interest. In the figure(a), object A is isolated (circled) and represented by a dot.

As noted in step 4 of the problem-solving strategy, we then construct the free-body diagram in the figure(b) using the same approach. Object B experiences two normal forces and two friction forces due to the presence of two contact surfaces. The interface with the inclined plane exerts external forces of NB and fB, and the interface with object B exerts the normal force NAB and friction fAB; NAB is directed away from object B, and fAB is opposing the tendency of the relative motion of object B with respect to object A.

(a) The free-body diagram for isolated object A. (b) The free-body diagram for isolated object B. Comparing the two drawings, we see that friction acts in the opposite direction in the two figures. Friction always acts opposite the direction of motion or intended motion. Because object A is moving to the right, friction by B must act to the left. Object B is moving to the left relative to B, so the friction by A on B is to the right. The friction force by object A on object B is the third law pair of the friction force by B on A, and therefore these two forces must be in opposite directions. Because object B is sliding down the incline, the friction force by the ramp must oppose it and act up the ramp.

Figure a shows two objects on an inclined plane, sloping down to the left. Object A is on top of object B. A free body diagram shows T pointing right and up, parallel to the plane, N subscript BA pointing left and up, perpendicular to the plane, f subscript BA pointing left and down, parallel to the plane and w subscript A pointing vertically down. W subscript A is weight of block A, T is tension, N subscript BA is normal force exerted by B on A, f subscript BA is friction force exerted by B on A. Figure b shows the objects on the slope in the same manner. A free body diagram has f subscript B and f subscript AB pointing right and up, parallel to the slope, N subscript B pointing left and up perpendicular to the slope, w subscript B pointing vertically down and N subscript AB pointing down and right, perpendicular to the slope. W subscript B is weight of block B, N subscript AB is normal force exerted by A on B, N subscript B is normal force exerted by the incline plane on B. f subscript AB is friction force exerted by A on B. f subscript B is friction force exerted by the incline plane on B.

We now include any force that acts on the body. Here, no applied force is present. The weight of the object acts as a force pointing vertically downward, and the presence of the cord indicates a force of tension pointing away from the object. Object A has one interface and hence experiences a normal force, directed away from the interface. The source of this force is object B, and this normal force is labeled accordingly. Since object B s sliding down and object A s sliding up with respect to the interface, so the friction fBA is directed downward parallel to the inclined plane.

interactions.label: Relative sliding tendency
interactions.teaches: Friction along a contact surface is set by the relative sliding tendency at that surface, so reversing the tendency reverses the friction arrows

demo_steps.title: Isolate one block
demo_steps.narration: Click block A or block B in the incline sketch. The selected block and its free-body diagram brighten, emphasizing that the diagram contains only forces acting on that block.

demo_steps.title: Compare the normal pair
demo_steps.narration: With the A-B normal pair highlighted, N_BA appears on block A while N_AB appears on block B. The arrows point in opposite perpendicular directions because each block pushes on the other.

demo_steps.title: Compare the friction pair
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the A-B friction pair. f_BA and f_AB are parallel to the contact surface but point in opposite directions, and they are placed on different isolated bodies.

demo_steps.title: Reverse the sliding tendency
demo_steps.narration: Change the relative sliding tendency and watch the friction arrows reverse along the contact surfaces. This shows that friction opposes relative motion, not simply motion to the left or right.

plan.keyInsight: The same contact produces two opposite forces, but each force must be drawn only on the free-body diagram of the object it acts on.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the figure as two horizontal textbook-style panels stacked vertically. In each panel, place the isolated red-arrow force diagram on the left, the small incline-and-block sketch in the middle, and the symbol-definition legend on the right. Use tan for the incline, tan for block B, salmon for block A, black for labels and cord, gray rounded outlines for the isolated body, and red arrows for forces. Keep the incline angle consistent across both panels. In click isolation mode, brighten the selected panel's isolated body outline and corresponding free-body diagram while fading the other body and unrelated arrows. In contact-pair mode, emphasize N_BA with N_AB for the normal pair or f_BA with f_AB for the friction pair using stronger red or glow, while other force arrows remain visible but muted. In sliding-tendency mode, reverse friction arrows along the A-B contact; also make clear that the incline friction on B depends on B's tendency relative to the plane.

discrepancies: The generated figure is squeezed beside a large control panel, causing the right-side explanatory legend text to be visibly clipped/truncated in the screenshot, whereas the source legend is fully readable.

evaluation.notes: The main two-panel free-body-diagram concept and force directions are recognizable, but the default rendering sacrifices textbook fidelity through clipped legend labels, oversized arrows, and compressed layout.
action_items: Resize or reposition the UI so the full 900px-wide textbook figure, especially the right-side legend definitions, remains fully visible and readable by default.
Reduce force-arrow stroke widths and arrowhead sizes to better match the source and lessen crowding around the central dots.
Reposition crowded vector labels in the lower free-body diagram so they do not overlap arrowheads, dashed reference lines, or nearby labels.
Tune the block and isolation-outline dimensions/positions to more closely match the source sketches.
